opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I find fascinating, because it seems almost paradoxical at first. If a norm is something everyone expects everyone else to follow, how does it get off the ground when nobody has that expectation yet?

The way I think about it is that agents don't need to start out sharing a convention. They need to start out sharing a willingness to *entertain* possible conventions. You come into a new situation with some prior sense of what rules might plausibly be in force. Maybe people drive on one side of the road, maybe there's a norm about taking turns at a shared resource, maybe there's a norm against taking more than your share. You're uncertain which, if any, actually holds.

Then you watch what others do, and you treat their behavior as evidence. If someone holds back from overharvesting even when it would benefit them in the short term, that's informative. It's more likely under a world where a norm against overharvesting exists than one where it doesn't. So you update toward that norm. And crucially, if you've updated toward it, you might start following it yourself, partly because you think it's what's expected and partly because you think others might sanction you if you don't.

That's where the experimentation comes in. Early on, agents act in ways that are partly exploratory. They try out behaviors consistent with candidate norms, and those behaviors become evidence for everyone else. There's a feedback loop: I act as if a norm might hold, you observe that and update toward it, you act accordingly, and I see your behavior as confirmation. Over time, beliefs that were initially diffuse can concentrate on a particular set of norms, and once enough agents believe in and comply with them, the norm becomes self-sustaining. It's real because people think it's real and act on it.

What I like about this framing is that it doesn't require some central authority or explicit negotiation. You get a kind of decentralized coordination through mutual inference. It also helps explain why conventions are often somewhat arbitrary. Which side of the road you drive on doesn't really matter, but once a population tips toward one, it locks in.

Of course, there are open questions. Not every norm that emerges this way is good. You can converge on conventions that are inefficient or unfair, and path dependence means early random behavior can shape outcomes a lot. So part of what I'm interested in is the conditions under which this process tends toward norms that actually serve people's interests, for example when agents have some prior bias toward norms that promote mutual benefit, or when there are mechanisms for revising norms that aren't working. That seems really relevant as we think about AI systems entering human social environments. We'd want them to pick up on our norms in this flexible way, without treating whatever they observe as automatically legitimate.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents trying behaviors consistent with candidate norms, others observing and updating, then acting accordingly; this feedback loop can establish a shared convention.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key move is to stop treating norms as things that have to be fully specified in advance, or that have to be derived from some fixed external criterion, and instead to see them as solutions to a coordination problem that agents can discover together through interaction.

If you think about it game-theoretically, a lot of situations have multiple equilibria. Which side of the road to drive on, how to split the work on a shared project, what counts as a fair division of some resource. There's no fact of the matter in advance about which one is "correct," but there's a very strong shared interest in landing on the same one. And what experimentation does is it lets agents probe each other. You try something, you see how the other party responds, and gradually you both update toward a pattern that's mutually acceptable. The key is that each agent is modeling the other agent as also trying to coordinate, and also having their own preferences. So it's not just trial and error, it's trial and error with a theory of mind in the loop.

I think there's an analogy to how children learn norms, actually. They don't get handed a rulebook. They try things, they get corrected, they watch what others do, they ask, and over time they internalize something that looks like a shared convention, even though nobody ever wrote it down. And crucially, they're learning not just what the rule is but that there is a rule, that others expect them to follow it, and that they can reasonably expect others to follow it too. That second-order structure, the mutual expectation, is what turns a behavioral regularity into a genuine norm.

From an AI perspective, what's exciting to me is that you can model this computationally. You can have agents that maintain uncertainty over what the norms might be, that take actions partly to reduce that uncertainty, and that treat other agents' behavior as evidence about what the norms are. And in multi-agent settings, you can show that populations of such agents will often converge on conventions even starting from nothing, and that the conventions they land on are shaped by things like who interacts with whom, how costly miscoordination is, and what prior each agent brings.

Now, I'd add a caveat, which is that experimentation can also produce bad conventions. Just because something is an equilibrium doesn't mean it's good. There are lots of stable norms that are unfair or inefficient, and history is full of them. So I don't think the story is "let agents experiment and whatever they land on is legitimate." I think it's more that experimentation is how you get the raw material of shared convention at all, and then you need other things, like deliberation, like the ability to renegotiate, like some baseline of equal standing, to make sure what you converge on is something that everyone could actually endorse. But without the experimental, interactive piece, you just don't get shared norms in the first place. You get rules imposed from outside, which is a different thing and often a much more brittle one.

r001.rationale: The response says agents experiment, observe others, and converge on conventions, and describes children watching and learning norms. It does not clearly state that imitation of people’s experimental rule-following generates the convention.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that experimenting with a norm changes the situation that everyone else is responding to. Even if we don’t start with a shared convention, I can try behaving according to some candidate rule, and you can see what happens and decide whether to reciprocate. If that makes our interaction more predictable or helps us coordinate, then we have a reason to keep doing it.

Suppose we’re sharing a workspace and there’s no agreement about who cleans up. One of us might propose taking turns, or just start doing something that makes that pattern apparent. We can then discover whether taking turns actually works for us, whether we understand it in the same way, and whether it feels fair. The proposal is a starting point for learning together.

There’s an important distinction, though, between a pattern of behavior and a norm. We might both happen to clean up regularly without thinking either of us owes that to the other. A norm starts to emerge when we develop a shared expectation that this is what we should do, and that departures call for some explanation. Experimentation can help us get there by making possible arrangements concrete enough to accept, contest, or revise.

r001.rationale: The response describes trying a candidate rule and others deciding whether to reciprocate, but it does not explain that imitation of experimental rule-following generates a shared convention.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that you don’t have to start with a shared convention. You can start with the ability to propose something, try it out, and observe how other people respond. Suppose we need to coordinate, but there’s no established rule for who does what. I might act according to one possible rule, and you might infer from my behavior what I’m trying to do. If you respond in a compatible way, we’ve got the beginnings of a convention.

But there’s a difference between accidentally coordinating once and establishing something we can both rely on. We need repeated interactions, or some communication, that makes our expectations mutually apparent. And we need opportunities to revise the rule if it works poorly for one of us.

So experimenting with norms is also experimenting with ways of living together. We discover which arrangements are feasible, which people are willing to accept, and which we can sustain. The shared convention emerges through that process of proposal, interpretation, and adjustment, rather than requiring everyone to agree on a complete set of rules beforehand.

r001.rationale: The response says one person can try a possible rule and another can infer it and respond compatibly. It does not explain that imitating people’s experimental rule-following generates the convention.
